{"id": "q106", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the interp-selected probe beat all three of its controls on Insider Trading Confirm but not on Sandbagging, how much support would that give the claim that the judge captures general deception directions?", "answer": "It would give little support. Confirm is easy for the baseline and leaves little headroom, so it discriminates poorly between rules. Sandbagging is the demanding, more revealing test, and failing there suggests the selection did not capture something general.", "rubric": ["Says it would be weak or little support", "Explains that Confirm has little headroom while Sandbagging is the more revealing test of generality"]},
{"id": "q107", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If Table 2's top source-probe PCs had mostly been high-index ones (for example PC80 to PC100), which explanation in Appendix D would be undermined?", "answer": "Appendix D's explanation would be undermined. It says the source probe's top PCs are low-index because low-index PCs capture the most source variance and the probe is trained on the same distribution. High-index top PCs would contradict this variance-based account, meaning the probe's reliance is not driven by variance.", "rubric": ["Identifies Appendix D's explanation that low-index dominance follows from those PCs capturing the most source variance", "Explains that high-index top-weighted PCs would contradict this variance-based account"]},
{"id": "q108", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the greedy reference on Sandbagging were barely above the full-representation baseline, what would follow for interpreting the interp rule's results on that target?", "answer": "The greedy probe indicates how much room any source-trained probe within the 100-PC basis has to improve. A small gap would mean little headroom on Sandbagging. The interp rule's comparisons there would then be uninformative, likely because the source basis covers the target poorly.", "rubric": ["Says there is little headroom, so the interp comparisons on Sandbagging would be uninformative", "Explains that greedy marks the attainable improvement for source-trained probes in the 100-PC basis (e.g., poor basis coverage of the target)"]},
{"id": "q109", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If the interp-selected PCs turned out to be exactly the top entries of Table 2 (PC7, PC8, PC11, ...), what would the interp rule fail to test that the paper motivates it to test?", "answer": "The paper motivates the interp rule by the possibility that transfer depends on a property not captured by discriminability on either domain. If the judge simply reproduced the source-probe ranking, the rule would amount to the source-discriminative hypothesis. It would add no test of any other property.", "rubric": ["Says the interp rule would collapse into the source-discriminative (source-PCA ranking) hypothesis", "Explains that it would then fail to probe a property beyond source or target discriminability, which is its stated motivation"]},
{"id": "q110", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the greedy search were run on target activations re-standardized with each target's own statistics, while the source-only rules used source statistics, which comparison would break?", "answer": "The use of greedy as a reference for the source-only rules would break. The rules would be operating on differently transformed representations, so greedy's advantage could partly come from target distribution information leaked through the standardization rather than from the PCs it chose. The paper fixes standardization on the source precisely to keep all rules comparable in what they see.", "rubric": ["Identifies the greedy-versus-source-only-rule comparison (greedy as reference) as broken", "Explains that target statistics would leak distribution information and make the representations non-comparable"]},
{"id": "q111", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs scored far above the greedy probe on Sandbagging, where would that place the bottleneck for transfer?", "answer": "The bottleneck would lie in how source-fit weights use the basis, not in basis coverage. A large gap would show that the 100-PC basis contains plenty of target-relevant signal. Yet even the best subset with source-fit weights cannot exploit it, because the weights are learned from Roleplaying.", "rubric": ["Says the basis contains the signal, so coverage is not the bottleneck", "Says the limit is source-fit weighting, since even optimal subset choice with source weights falls short"]},
{"id": "q112", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If Appendix E had shown the judge routinely describing narrow, specific patterns as broad sentiment or honesty directions, which design goal of the judge prompt would have failed, and what would that mean for the OOD scores?", "answer": "The goal of preventing overgeneralization, which the prompt targets by asking for the narrowest accurate description, would have failed. Narrow directions would then look general and could receive inflated OOD scores. The scores would no longer reliably separate general strategies from local patterns.", "rubric": ["Identifies the anti-overgeneralization goal (narrowest accurate description)", "Explains that inflated generality would make the OOD scores unreliable for selecting general directions"]},
{"id": "q113", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that selecting subspaces in the source PCA basis transfers better than selecting individual raw activation dimensions? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper adopts the PC basis to avoid assuming the model's latent dimensions are privileged, and argues that it is convenient: it is computed from the source, has bipolar directions, and gives orthogonal subsets. It never runs selection over raw dimensions for comparison.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the PC basis is chosen on conceptual and practical grounds and no raw-dimension selection comparison is run"]},
{"id": "q114", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that mean-pooling over assistant tokens is the best way to aggregate activations for transferable deception probes? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Mean-pooling over the assistant response is a fixed condition of the setup, and no alternative aggregation is compared.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that mean-pooling is a fixed setup choice with no comparison to alternatives"]},
{"id": "q115", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that layer 15 is the best layer for its PC-subspace selection procedures? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Layer 15 is borrowed from Ying et al., where it had the highest cross-domain AUROC in their analysis. This paper evaluates no other layers, and it lists other readout locations as an open question.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the layer was taken from prior work's cross-domain AUROC and no other layers are tested here"]},
{"id": "q116", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its PC-subspace selections would also help nonlinear probes generalize? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The pipeline is fully linear, consisting of a PCA projection followed by logistic regression. The paper explicitly leaves extension to nonlinear probes as an open question.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that only linear probes are used and nonlinear extension is stated as open"]},
{"id": "q117", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that removing GPT-4o's ambiguous responses improves probe transfer? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Removing ambiguous responses is a preprocessing step applied throughout. No configuration that keeps them is evaluated, so its effect on transfer is never measured.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that removal is applied uniformly and there is no comparison with ambiguous responses kept"]},
{"id": "q118", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper present the target-PCA probe ranking as a selection method that can be deployed without labeled target data? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. The ranking comes from a probe trained on target labels, and its k is set by a greedy run that uses target labels. It serves as a hypothesis test, and the paper reserves the deployable, target-free role for the interp rule.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Explains that the ranking relies on a target-trained probe (target labels), unlike the source-only interp rule"]},
{"id": "q119", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does a low Jaccard overlap between two selection rules' PC sets (Appendix D) show that the two rules give probes with different target AUROC? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Appendix D presents Jaccard overlap as a measure of how far two rules draw on the same directions. Overlap describes set membership, not performance, and the paper does not show that low overlap implies different AUROC.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that Jaccard measures shared directions, not performance, and no link to AUROC is established"]}
]}

{"id": "q121", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "The first hypothesis in Section 4.3 concerns PCs that separate the target classes well by themselves, but the target-PCA probe ranking uses weights from a single probe fit on all PCs jointly. {"id": "q122", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If the ranking-based probes of Section 4.3 were compared against the AUROC of the full-target greedy run used to set k, rather than against the per-fold greedy reference, why would that comparison be misleading?", "answer": "The full-target greedy run selects PCs using AUROC on all target examples and has no held-out fold. Its AUROC is therefore measured on the very data used for selection, which makes it more optimistically inflated than the per-fold reference. Against this inflated bar, the ranking rules would look worse than they really are.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the full-target greedy AUROC would be an inflated (overly optimistic) reference", "Reason: its subset is selected and evaluated on the same target examples, with no held-out fold"]},
{"id": "q123", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "On what kind of target could the judge's scoring instructions make the interp-selected probe do worse than the full-representation baseline, and why?", "answer": "A target close to Roleplaying that reuses its wording, lexical markers or style. The judge is told to give low scores to surface cues, lexical habits and task-specific phrasing, so the interp subspace discards those directions. On a near-source target those directions would actually transfer, and the baseline keeps them. On such targets the baseline also has little headroom.", "rubric": ["Identifies a target near the source that shares Roleplaying's lexical, stylistic or phrasing cues", "Reason: the judge scores such surface-cue directions low, so the interp subspace drops directions that would transfer there, while the baseline keeps them"]},
{"id": "q124", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "When would both the interp-selected probe and the complement-control probe retain the same transferable signal, blurring what the complement control shows?", "answer": "This happens when the transferable direction does not line up with individual PCs but is a linear mix spread over both selected and unselected PCs. Each orthogonal subspace then keeps part of that direction's projection. Both probes can transfer partially, so the comparison cannot cleanly attribute the signal to either set.", "rubric": ["Identifies the condition: the transferable direction is spread across selected and unselected PCs rather than aligned with individual PCs", "Reason: each subspace retains part of its projection, so both probes can carry the signal and the comparison cannot attribute it cleanly"]},
{"id": "q125", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "The Limitations say the two-run agreement filter mitigates only some of the judge's variability. Which kind of variability can it not remove, and why?", "answer": "It cannot remove systematic bias that recurs across runs. Both runs use the same judge model, the same prompt and the same exemplars, so a direction the judge consistently over-rates will pass the agreement check. The filter only removes run-to-run sampling noise.", "rubric": ["Identifies systematic or consistent bias (from the judge model, prompt or exemplars) as the variability not removed", "Reason: both runs share the same model, prompt and examples, so consistent misjudgments survive the agreement requirement; only random run-to-run noise is filtered"]},
{"id": "q126", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the source-PCA probe ranking mechanically tilted toward high-variance PCs while the judge's OOD score is not?", "answer": "The standardized coefficient multiplies each weight by the PC's standard deviation, and that standard deviation falls with PC index. The judge instead sees activations normalized per direction to integers from -10 to +10, and only for extreme examples, so it gets no information about a PC's variance. Any preference the judge shows for low-index PCs could only arise indirectly, for example because they are more interpretable (Appendix C).", "rubric": ["States that the standardized coefficient includes the PC's standard deviation, which is larger for low-index PCs", "States that the judge sees per-direction activations normalized to -10..+10 for extreme examples, with no variance information", "Notes that any judge tilt would be indirect, for example via interpretability or SAE alignment"]},
{"id": "q127", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "The judge's output never says which pole of a PC corresponds to deception. Why does the interp rule not need that information?", "answer": "The judge only decides which directions the probe may use. The logistic regression is then fit on source labels over the projected activations, so it learns the sign and size of the weight on each selected PC itself.", "rubric": ["States that the probe learns each PC's sign and weight from labeled source data", "States that the judge's role is only to choose which directions are allowed, not how they are used"]},
{"id": "q128", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the judge prompt's instruction to give lexical habits and task-specific phrasing low scores well matched to the paper's deception targets?", "answer": "The targets (a misleading trading report, a confirmation denial, deliberately wrong answers) share little vocabulary or structure with Roleplaying's roleplayed excuses. Directions tied to Roleplaying's wording are therefore expected not to recur on the targets, and the paper argues that a probe latching onto one setting's vocabulary fails on the others.", "rubric": ["States that the targets share little vocabulary or structure with Roleplaying", "Reason: directions tied to source wording are therefore unlikely to transfer, so penalizing them targets the expected failure mode"]},
{"id": "q129", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why do the target datasets also need their ambiguous responses removed, not just Roleplaying, for the paper's evaluations to work?", "answer": "Target evaluation and the greedy selection both use AUROC over honest (0) versus deceptive (1) labels. Ambiguous (-1) responses belong to neither class, so they cannot be counted as positives or negatives in that AUROC.", "rubric": ["States that ambiguous target responses cannot be scored as either class", "Reason: target evaluation and greedy selection use binary honest-versus-deceptive AUROC"]},
{"id": "q130", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the interp procedure show the judge both the most and the least activating examples of each PC, rather than only top-activating ones as in neuron-explanation work?", "answer": "Each PC is a bipolar direction, and a linear probe uses the whole axis. What a PC encodes is therefore the contrast between its two poles, and describing one pole alone cannot say what moving along the direction means. The deception-relevant behavior could also sit at the negative pole.", "rubric": ["States that PCs are bipolar directions whose meaning is a contrast between two poles", "Reason: the probe uses the full axis, so one pole alone does not characterize the direction (the relevant behavior may lie at the negative pole)"]},
{"id": "q131", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to rerun the interp rule over the top 400 Roleplaying PCs, with the same ambiguous-label filtering. Can this work, and why?", "answer": "No. After the 59 ambiguous responses are removed, Roleplaying has 312 examples. PCA on 312 centered examples has at most 311 directions with nonzero variance, so a basis of 400 meaningful source PCs cannot exist.", "rubric": ["Concludes that 400 meaningful source PCs are not available", "Reason: only 312 usable Roleplaying examples remain, so PCA yields at most about 311 nonzero-variance components"]},
{"id": "q132", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If Insider Trading Report were merged into the source alongside Roleplaying, which of the remaining targets would still be a clearly OOD test, and why?", "answer": "Only Sandbagging. Report is no longer held out. Insider Trading Confirm shares Report's insider-trading scenario, so it would become close to the source distribution. Sandbagging differs from both source datasets in topic and in the form of deception.", "rubric": ["Concludes that Sandbagging is the only clearly OOD target left", "Reason: Insider Trading Confirm shares Report's scenario (and Report is no longer held out), while Sandbagging differs in topic and in the form of deception"]},
{"id": "q133", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the interp rule kept PC2, PC40 and PC55. Which PCs would the matched-size variance control and the complement control contain, and which PCs would those two controls have in common?", "answer": "The matched-size control uses PC1, PC2 and PC3. The complement uses the other 97 of the top 100 PCs, everything except PC2, PC40 and PC55. The two controls share PC1 and PC3, and the matched-size control also shares PC2 with the interp subset.", "rubric": ["Matched-size control = PC1–PC3; complement = the 97 remaining top-100 PCs (all except PC2, PC40, PC55)", "States that the two controls share PC1 and PC3"]},
{"id": "q134", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to reuse the paper's framework to study probe transfer for refusal instead of deception. Which selection procedure needs substantive redesign rather than just new data, and why?", "answer": "The interp rule. Its judge prompt is deception-specific: it describes the source setup as a chance to lie, rates 'OOD deception usefulness', and reserves scores of 5 or more for deception-relevant strategies. The greedy search, the two weight-based rankings and the controls do not depend on the behavior; they only need new source and target data with labels.", "rubric": ["Identifies the interp rule (its judge prompt) as needing redesign", "Reason: the prompt and scoring criteria are written specifically about deception, whereas greedy, the weight rankings and the controls work for any behavior given labeled data"]},
{"id": "q135", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A team adopts the interp rule for a domain with no labeled examples and wants to check it against the paper's three controls before deployment. What can and cannot they do?", "answer": "They can train all three control probes, because each is trained only on source data. They cannot tell on the target whether the interp probe beats the controls, because that comparison needs target AUROC and therefore target labels. At most they can compare the probes in-distribution on Roleplaying.", "rubric": ["States that the control probes can be built without target data", "States that comparing them on the target is impossible without target labels, since evaluation requires labeled AUROC"]},
{"id": "q136", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A team has 10 labeled target examples, 2 of them deceptive, and wants to compute the paper's per-fold greedy reference. What goes wrong?", "answer": "With 5 folds, each held-out fold has 2 examples, and at most two folds can contain a deceptive example. Most held-out folds therefore contain only one class, where AUROC is undefined. The selection folds are also tiny, so the AUROC improvements that drive the search would be very noisy.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the reference cannot be computed properly: most held-out folds lack one of the two classes, so AUROC is undefined", "Reason: 10 examples split into 5 folds gives 2 per fold, and only 2 deceptive examples exist (selection folds are also too small to guide the search)"]},
{"id": "q137", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If neither the source-PCA probe ranking nor the target-PCA probe ranking had behaved like the greedy reference, which part of the paper would gain support?", "answer": "The motivation for the interpretability-driven rule would gain support. Both discriminability hypotheses would have failed, which points to transfer depending on some property of directions that discriminability on neither domain captures. That is exactly the possibility the paper says motivates the interpretability analysis.", "rubric": ["Identifies the motivation for the interpretability-driven rule or analysis as strengthened", "Reason: failure of both rankings suggests transfer depends on a property not captured by source or target discriminability"]},
{"id": "q138", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the greedy subsets for Insider Trading Report and Insider Trading Confirm turned out nearly identical, what would that suggest about the factor that distinguishes those two targets?", "answer": "The two targets share a scenario and differ mainly in whether deception is an initial omission or a later explicit confirmation. Nearly identical subsets would suggest that this difference in the form of the deceptive act barely changes which source directions transfer, and that the shared scenario or a shared deception signal dominates. Because Confirm is easy for the baseline, the evidence would be limited.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the omission-versus-confirmation difference has little effect on which directions transfer", "Reason: the two targets share a scenario and differ mainly in that form of deceptive act", "Optionally caveats that Confirm's easiness or small size limits the inference"]},
{"id": "q139", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "If the judge's top-scored PCs had been mostly those with the weakest SAE decoder alignment in Appendix C, what would that undermine?", "answer": "It would undermine trust in those specific OOD scores. The top-100 restriction is justified by the idea that the directions are interpretable enough to be described in natural language. Top scores going to the least SAE-aligned PCs would mean the judge's highest ratings rest on descriptions of the directions that are hardest to interpret.", "rubric": ["Identifies reliability of the judge's top scores (or the interpretability premise behind them) as undermined", "Reason: the top-100 restriction is meant to ensure directions can be described, and the least-aligned PCs are the least describable"]},
{"id": "q140", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the three target datasets shared much of Roleplaying's vocabulary and structure, which stated rationale for using deception as the testbed would weaken?", "answer": "The rationale that deception makes the gap between in-distribution and OOD behavior especially visible would weaken. That rationale rests on the targets sharing little vocabulary, so that a vocabulary-latching probe fails. With shared vocabulary, lexical probes could transfer, and the reason to penalize lexical directions would also weaken.", "rubric": ["Identifies the rationale that deception makes the in-distribution versus OOD gap visible", "Reason: that rationale relies on targets sharing little vocabulary, so that vocabulary-latching probes fail"]},
{"id": "q141", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the judge described Table 2's top PCs (PC7, PC8, PC11, PC12) mostly as lexical or stylistic surface cues, which claim from the paper's motivation would this support, and with what limitation?", "answer": "It would support the claim that probes trained on source representations combine general behavioral features with dataset-specific surface cues, because the directions the source probe leans on most would look like surface cues. It would also count against the idea that simply compacting the source signal fixes transfer. The evidence would be only descriptive, since there is no causal validation of what PCs encode.", "rubric": ["Identifies support for the claim that source-trained probes rely on surface cues mixed with general features", "Limitation: the judge's descriptions are descriptive only, with no causal validation"]},
{"id": "q142", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the interp-selected probe matched the per-fold greedy reference on Sandbagging, what would that imply, and what caveat would apply?", "answer": "It would imply that a rule using no target data recovers nearly all the transfer achievable by a source-trained probe within the 100-PC basis, on the most demanding target. That would be the strongest evidence for the interp rule as a deployable method. The caveat is that this is a single distant target, and the bound holds only within the 100-PC basis.", "rubric": ["Concludes that the target-free rule reaches near the achievable transfer within the basis, strongly supporting it as a deployable method", "Caveat: a single distant target, so conclusions need caution (and the bound is relative to the 100-PC basis)"]},
{"id": "q143", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If a selection rule fails on Sandbagging, does the paper let one conclude that the failure is caused by the change in the form of deception? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Sandbagging differs from Roleplaying in both topic and form of deception, so the two factors are confounded. The paper also warns that conclusions from a single distant target should be treated with caution.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: Sandbagging differs in both topic and form, so the two are confounded (and it is a single distant target)"]},
{"id": "q144", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that Sandbagging is harder for the full-representation baseline than Insider Trading Report? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper calls Sandbagging the most out-of-distribution target, but distance from the source is not the same as measured difficulty. The only baseline-difficulty statement the paper makes is that Insider Trading Confirm is easy.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: Sandbagging is described as most distant, not shown to be hardest; the only difficulty statement concerns Confirm being easy"]},
{"id": "q145", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that a decision threshold chosen on Roleplaying would give acceptable false-positive rates on Insider Trading Report? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Transfer is assessed with AUROC, which reflects ranking quality, not a fixed threshold. The base rates also differ sharply: Roleplaying is about 55% deceptive after filtering (172/312), while Report is about 24% (61/255). Threshold transfer is never tested.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: only AUROC-based evaluation is used and thresholded behavior is never tested, while deceptive base rates differ (about 55% versus about 24%)"]},
{"id": "q146", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that PCs given high OOD scores by the judge are also the PCs with the largest source-probe standardized coefficients? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Table 2 lists source-probe weights, but the paper never reports which PCs the judge scores highly or how those scores relate to the weights. The judge also never sees labels or weights.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: no comparison between judge scores and source-probe weights is reported (the judge does not use weights or labels)"]},
{"id": "q147", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that source PCs beyond the top 100 contain no transferable deception signal? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The top-100 cutoff is justified only by interpretability, and the authors explicitly do not claim that low-index PCs generalize better. No experiment examines PCs beyond index 100.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: the cutoff is an interpretability choice, not a generalization claim, and PCs beyond 100 are never tested"]},
{"id": "q148", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does Appendix C show that each of the top 100 PCs corresponds to a single SAE feature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Appendix C reports only rank correlations between PC index and decoder alignment, both for the best-matching feature and for the mean of the top 10 features. It gives no absolute alignment levels that would show a one-to-one correspondence.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Reason: only Spearman correlations of alignment with PC index are reported, not alignment magnitudes or one-to-one matches"]},
{"id": "q149", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could the per-fold greedy PC subsets of Section 4.2 change if the target cross-validation used 10 folds instead of 5?", "answer": "Yes. Selection runs on the non-held-out target folds, and with 10 folds those selection sets are different. The selected subsets could therefore differ.", "rubric": ["Answers yes, they can change", "Reason: per-fold selection uses the non-held-out folds, which change with the fold split"]},
{"id": "q150", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could the k used by the weight-based rankings in Section 4.3 change if the target cross-validation used 10 folds instead of 5?", "answer": "No. k comes from a greedy run on the full target dataset rather than from the per-fold runs, so the fold split does not affect it.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reason: k is set by a greedy run on the full target dataset, independent of the cross-validation folds"]},
{"id": "q151", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Could the number of PCs used by the source-PCA probe ranking rule change if the greedy stopping threshold were raised from 0.001 to 0.01?", "answer": "Yes. That number is k, which is set by the full-target greedy run, and that run's length depends on the stopping threshold. A higher threshold stops the search earlier, giving the same or a smaller k.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reason: k comes from the full-target greedy run, whose stopping depends on the threshold"]},
{"id": "q152", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Could the number of PCs in the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance control of Section 4.5 change if the greedy stopping threshold were raised from 0.001 to 0.01?", "answer": "No. That control's size is matched to the interp-selected subset, which is determined by the judge's scores and does not involve the greedy search.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reason: its size is matched to the interp-selected subset, which does not depend on greedy"]},
{"id": "q153", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Would the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs change if some non-ambiguous Roleplaying examples had their honest/deceptive labels flipped?", "answer": "No. That probe uses Roleplaying only for the standardization statistics and the PCA basis, and neither uses labels. Its weights are fit on target labels.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reason: the source contributes only label-free standardization and PCA, and the probe is fit on target labels"]},
{"id": "q154", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "Would the target-trained probe on the top-100 source PCs change if the ambiguous Roleplaying responses were kept instead of removed?", "answer": "Yes. Keeping those responses changes the source mean and variance used to standardize targets, and it changes the PCA basis. The target activations are therefore projected onto different directions before the probe is fit.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Reason: the extra source examples change the standardization statistics and the PCA basis that target data is projected onto"]},
{"id": "q155", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the judge had given every PC exactly one point more in both runs, with no score exceeding 10, would the interp-selected subset change?", "answer": "No. The rule keeps PCs that received the highest observed score in both runs, which is a relative criterion. A uniform shift leaves the same PCs at the top of each run.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Reason: selection uses the highest observed score (relative), so a uniform shift preserves which PCs are top-scored"]},
{"id": "q156", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If, with the judge's scores unchanged, the rule instead kept every PC scoring 5 or more in both runs, would the interp-selected subset change?", "answer": "Yes, in general. An absolute cutoff at 5 adds any PCs scoring at least 5 but below the maximum. It would also return nothing if the maximum were below 5. It matches the current rule only when exactly the top-scored PCs reach 5.", "rubric": ["Answers yes (in general)", "Reason: an absolute threshold differs from the relative highest-observed-score rule, adding PCs scoring at least 5 but below the maximum (or excluding all if the maximum is below 5)"]}
]}

{"items": [
{"id": "q155", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "When would the interpretability-driven rule miss a genuinely general deception contrast even though that contrast lies entirely within the top 100 source PCs?", "answer": "It would miss the contrast if the contrast were spread obliquely across several PCs instead of aligned with any single one. The judge describes and scores each PC on its own from that PC's extreme examples, so each PC would show only a mixed or partial pattern and get a low or noisy score. The agreement filter would then drop such PCs.", "rubric": ["Asserts the failure occurs when the general contrast is spread across several PCs rather than aligned with one PC", "Explains that the judge scores PCs one at a time from their own extreme examples, so each PC looks mixed or noisy and receives a low score"]},
{"id": "q156", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "For the target-PCA probe ranking, the paper does not say whether the PC standard deviation in the standardized coefficient is measured on source or on target projections. When would this choice change which PCs are selected?", "answer": "The choice matters when a PC's spread on the target differs substantially from its spread on Roleplaying. Target activations are standardized with source statistics, not their own, so target variance along a PC need not match source variance. Using one standard deviation or the other then rescales the coefficients differently and can reorder the top-k.", "rubric": ["Asserts the ranking changes when PC variances differ between source and target projections", "Explains that targets are standardized with source statistics, so their variance along a PC is not forced to match the source variance, and the multiplier therefore reorders PCs"]},
{"id": "q157", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "When would the source-PCA probe ranking be a weak test of the source-discriminative hypothesis, even if that hypothesis were true?", "answer": "It is a weak test when the source probe spreads its weight fairly evenly over many PCs with similar standardized coefficients. The top-k is then decided by small, unstable differences, so the PCs kept are nearly arbitrary. A mismatch with greedy would then say little about the hypothesis.", "rubric": ["Asserts the test is weak when standardized coefficients are similar across many PCs (weight spread evenly)", "Explains that the top-k cut then depends on small, unstable differences, making the selected set near-arbitrary"]},
{"id": "q158", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the full-target greedy run for some target returned a k close to 100, why could the Section 4.3 comparison not distinguish its two hypotheses?", "answer": "Both rankings would then pick nearly the whole 100-PC basis, so their top-k sets would largely coincide. Both resulting source-trained probes would be close to the source probe on all top-100 PCs. Their AUROCs would be almost identical regardless of which hypothesis is true.", "rubric": ["Asserts the two ranking-based probes would be nearly identical, so the hypotheses cannot be separated", "Explains that with k near 100 both top-k sets cover almost all PCs and approximate the top-100 source probe"]},
{"id": "q159", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "When would the interpretability-driven rule's design, by itself, prevent it from matching the greedy reference on all three targets at once?", "answer": "This happens when different targets depend on different source directions. Sandbagging's deliberately wrong answers might need different PCs than Insider Trading Confirm's explicit confirmations, for example. The interp rule yields one target-free subspace for all targets, while greedy picks a separate subset per target, so one fixed subspace cannot be best everywhere.", "rubric": ["Asserts this occurs when the targets rely on different source directions", "Explains that the interp rule produces a single subspace for all targets, whereas greedy is tailored to each target"]},
{"id": "q160", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "When would beating the matched-size top-PCs-by-variance control in Section 4.5 be weak evidence that the judge picked good directions?", "answer": "It would be weak evidence if the highest-variance PCs carried little deception signal at all, since almost any other subset of that size would then beat them. Table 2 suggests this is not trivially true on the source: the source probe leans heavily on low-index PCs such as PC2 through PC8. Whether that holds on targets is not shown.", "rubric": ["Asserts the evidence is weak when top-variance PCs carry little deception signal, so any other subset would win", "Notes that Table 2 shows the source probe relies heavily on low-index PCs, so the control is not trivially weak on the source"]},
{"id": "q161", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can the greedy reference avoid adding a PC whose source-fit weight points the wrong way for the target, while the target-PCA probe ranking cannot?", "answer": "Greedy scores each candidate by the target AUROC of a probe fit on source data. A PC whose source-learned sign works against the target lowers that AUROC, so greedy does not add it. The target-PCA ranking orders PCs by the absolute standardized coefficient of a probe fit on target data, which ignores whether the later source fit will get the sign right.", "rubric": ["Asserts that greedy evaluates candidates with the source-fit probe on target AUROC, so wrong-sign PCs reduce AUROC and are not added", "Explains that the target-PCA ranking uses absolute coefficients from a target-fit probe and so ignores how the source fit will orient each PC"]},
{"id": "q162", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why might an interp-selected probe score lower on held-out Roleplaying data than the source probe on all top-100 PCs, even if it transfers better?", "answer": "The judge deliberately gives low scores to lexical and stylistic directions, even when they look clean within the source data (Appendix E). Discarding those directions removes signal that genuinely separates Roleplaying classes. In-distribution accuracy can therefore fall even while out-of-distribution robustness improves.", "rubric": ["Asserts that in-distribution performance can drop because source-discriminative directions are discarded", "Explains that the judge penalizes lexical or stylistic directions even when they are clean or predictive within the source data"]},
{"id": "q163", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the judge prompt state the source setup (Roleplay in a simple scenario with a strategic chance to lie) alongside the examples?", "answer": "Knowing the setup lets the judge recognize which wording comes from the Roleplaying task itself. That is what it needs in order to follow the instruction to give low scores to task-specific phrasing that merely correlates with deception in these examples. Without the setup, scenario wording could be mistaken for a general strategy.", "rubric": ["Asserts that the setup helps the judge identify task-specific or scenario-specific phrasing", "Links this to the prompt's instruction to give low scores to task-specific cues that only correlate with deception in the source"]},
{"id": "q164", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "For the same target, why can the top-k-by-variance control in Section 4.2 and the matched-size variance control in Section 4.5 contain different numbers of PCs?", "answer": "The two controls are matched to different procedures. The Section 4.2 control matches the size of the greedy subset, which depends on the target fold. The Section 4.5 control matches the number of PCs the judge kept, which is fixed and independent of the target.", "rubric": ["Asserts that the two controls are matched to different reference sets", "States that one is sized by the greedy subset (target-dependent) and the other by the interp-selected count (target-free)"]},
{"id": "q165", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can every PC in a greedy subset be given a natural-language description without any extra interpretation work?", "answer": "Greedy searches only over the top 100 source PCs. Section 4.4 already ran the judge on each of those 100 PCs. Every PC greedy selects therefore already has pole descriptions and an OOD score that can be read direction by direction.", "rubric": ["Asserts that descriptions already exist for every PC greedy can pick", "Explains that greedy draws only from the top 100 PCs and the judge described all top 100 PCs"]},
{"id": "q166", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would the target-PCA probe ranking's probe and the full-target greedy probe give exactly the same target AUROC whenever their PC sets coincide?", "answer": "In both cases the final probe is a logistic regression with lambda=10 fit on source activations projected onto the selected PCs. The same set of PCs therefore yields the same probe weights and the same target scores. How each set was ranked or found does not matter.", "rubric": ["Asserts the probes would be identical", "Explains that both are fit on source data with the same regularization on the same projected subspace, so only set identity matters"]},
{"id": "q167", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could the number of PCs in the Section 4.2 top-k-by-variance control differ across the five CV folds of a single target?", "answer": "Yes. k is matched to the greedy subset selected in each fold, and greedy runs separately on each fold's non-held-out data, so its subset size can vary.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that k matches the per-fold greedy subset size, which can vary because selection uses different target folds"]},
{"id": "q168", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Could the number of PCs in the Section 4.5 matched-size variance control differ across Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm and Sandbagging?", "answer": "No. Its size matches the interp-selected subset, which comes from source-only judge scores. That subset is the same for every target, so the control's size is too.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that the size is matched to the interp subset, which uses no target data and is the same for all targets"]},
{"id": "q169", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Would the full-representation baseline probe change if activations were taken from layer 20 instead of layer 15?", "answer": "Yes. The baseline is trained directly on the layer's standardized activations, so different activations give a different probe.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that the baseline is trained on the activations themselves, which would be different"]},
{"id": "q170", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Would the full-representation baseline probe change if the judge were shown 16 rather than 8 most and least activating examples per PC?", "answer": "No. The baseline is trained on full standardized source activations and never uses PCA or judge scores, so changing the judge's exemplars cannot affect it.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that the baseline does not depend on the judge or PC selection"]},
{"id": "q171", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If only the top 50 source PCs were retained instead of 100, would the full-representation baseline probe change?", "answer": "No. The baseline trains directly on the full standardized activations, not on PC projections, so the number of PCs retained does not enter it.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that the baseline uses full standardized activations rather than the PC basis"]},
{"id": "q172", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If only the top 50 source PCs were retained instead of 100, would the target-trained probe used as a reference configuration change?", "answer": "Yes. That probe is trained on target data projected onto the retained source PCs, so halving the subspace changes its inputs and generally its fit.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that the target-trained probe operates within the retained PC subspace, which would shrink"]},
{"id": "q173", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If PCs were ranked by raw absolute coefficients rather than by coefficient times PC standard deviation, could the source-PCA probe ranking's selected PCs change?", "answer": "Yes. PC standard deviations differ, falling with index, so removing that multiplier can reorder PCs and change which ones fall in the top-k.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that PCs have different standard deviations, so removing the multiplier can reorder the ranking"]},
{"id": "q174", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If PCs were ranked by raw absolute coefficients rather than by coefficient times PC standard deviation, could the per-fold greedy subsets of Section 4.2 change?", "answer": "No. Greedy adds PCs by their improvement in target AUROC and never uses a probe-coefficient ranking, so changing the ranking metric does not affect it.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that greedy selection depends on target AUROC gains, not on coefficient rankings"]},
{"id": "q175", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p5", "question": "Would the greedy reference still measure how well a source-trained probe could transfer if, at each step, probe weights were refit on Roleplaying data with lambda=1 instead of lambda=10?", "answer": "Yes. The weights would still come only from source data, with only the regularization strength changed. It would still be a diagnostic of source-trained transfer, though possibly with different subsets and AUROCs.", "rubric": ["Answers yes", "Explains that weights are still fit on source data, so it remains a source-trained transfer diagnostic"]},
{"id": "q176", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p5", "question": "Would the greedy reference still measure how well a source-trained probe could transfer if, at each step, probe weights were refit on the non-held-out target folds?", "answer": "No. The weights would then be learned from target labels, so the procedure would be measuring a target-trained probe within the selected PCs rather than how far a source-trained probe can transfer.", "rubric": ["Answers no", "Explains that fitting weights on target data turns it into a target-trained probe rather than a test of source-trained transfer"]},
{"id": "q177", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "A team wants to replace source PCs with SAE decoder features as the basis for the paper's selection rules. Which property that the paper relies on for clean comparisons and ablations would they lose?", "answer": "They would lose orthogonality. A subset of PCs defines an orthogonal subspace, so restricting to a set or to its complement cleanly separates directions. SAE decoder features are generally not mutually orthogonal, so controls such as the complement of the selected set would no longer cleanly remove the selected directions.", "rubric": ["Identifies orthogonality of the selected directions as the lost property", "Explains that, without orthogonality, training on subsets or complements (such as the complement control) no longer cleanly includes or excludes the selected directions"]},
